[MUQATIL:34:24/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The question addresses Meccan idolaters who worship angels: rain comes from heaven and plants from earth.
[MUQATIL:34:24/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Meccans answered Allah, with we are provided understood; the Prophet is told to say that God provides for you, then the speech breaks off. | mentions 10:31
[MUQATIL:34:24/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · كفار مكة | reports | The Meccans proposed comparing worldly livelihoods and told Muhammad and his companions they were astray.
[MUQATIL:34:24/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Muhammad and his companions are the guided party, while the Meccan unbelievers are in manifest error; one of the two groups must be so.
[MUQATIL:34:24/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The alif here is extra, as in the wording cited from 25:44. | mentions 25:44
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p759/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The Prophet is told to ask the polytheists who provides for them from the heavens and the earth.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p759/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The answer to the question of who provides is God.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p759/r6] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The phrasing says that one of the two groups, the believers or their opponents, is guided and the other plainly astray.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p759/r7] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · ابن مجاهد عن أبيه | reports | Ibn Mujāhid's father says the intended contrast is that we are guided and you are astray; this indirect Arab idiom lets a speaker imply himself as truthful, or his companion as the liar, fitting the Muslims' weakness in Mecca.
[MAJAZ:v2p148/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | He paraphrases it as we are guided and you are in manifest error; Arabs can use aw where a coordinating wāw joins the paired terms, as in the cited line.
[MAJAZ:v2p148/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · قوم | reports | Some say a speaker certain of his own faith uses this balanced wording sarcastically, knowing which side is guided; Abū al-Aswad’s conditional poem illustrates the posture.
[AKHFASH:v2p483#2/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | This is not uncertainty: Arabic presents two sides while meaning that the speaker is guided; a master can say one of us is striking his companion and be understood as the striker.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p357/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The wording is a tactful challenge: one party is wrong, although each side knows the other is wrong and itself is right.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p357/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda paraphrases the phrase directly: you are guided and your group is in manifest error.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p166/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Al-Farrāʾ attributes the balanced alternative to indirect address: one of us is astray and one guided, while God knows the Messenger is guided and his opponents astray; it tactfully says one of us lies.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p166/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The indirect phrasing resembles telling someone who contradicts you that one of us must be lying, while intending him without bluntly naming him.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The question points to God’s provision through rain, crops and livelihoods, the sun, moon and stars, and food produced by the earth for people and livestock.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The expected answer is initially omitted because the question makes it clear, then supplied as God; if the idolaters say they do not know, Muhammad is to say it.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The wording tells the opponents that either the speakers are guided or astray, or the opponents are; one side must be astray.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says Muhammad’s companions told the polytheists that they were not both on one course and one of the two groups was guided.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عكرمة وزياد | reports | Ikrima and Ziyad make the implied contrast explicit: we are guided and you are plainly astray.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي البصرة | reports | A Basran grammarian says أو does not express doubt: in ordinary speech, saying one of us struck the other can make clear that the master struck his servant.
[TAB-FULL:v19p283#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · آخر منهم | reports | Another Basran grammarian says Arabs sometimes use أو like the conjunction واو; Jarir’s line means Thalaba and Riyah, supporting an assured but indirect formulation.
[TAB-FULL:v19p285/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | An anonymous wāfir poem is cited in the same discussion as an example of conditional alternatives phrased so the speaker can state either outcome without conceding error.
[TAB-FULL:v19p285/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي الكوفة | reports | A Kufan grammarian discusses أو as equivalent in sense to واو here, while distinguishing it from free conjunction: in a delegated choice such as one or two dirhams, the listener may take either one or two, but not three.
[TAB-FULL:v19p285/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي الكوفة | reports | The grammarian explains the line as tactful denial: a speaker who knows his opponent lies can say one of us is a liar, and Arab expressions can soften a direct rebuke.
[TAB-FULL:v19p285/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers that God instructs Muhammad to refute the opponents graciously: saying one of us is lying means the interlocutor, not the Prophet himself.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p252/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Exegetes take the wording to mean that the speaker is guided and the opponents are clearly astray, though Zajjāj says that is not valid as a literal linguistic construction.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p252/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The wording presents either side as possibly guided or astray; the intended force is that one of two parties is truthful and the other false.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p252/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | He illustrates the indirect formulation with the idiom that one of two people is truthful and one a liar, without naming which.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Man is a complete interrogative noun in the nominative as subject, and yarzuqukum is its predicate.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The qāf may assimilate into the kāf, changing the qāf into a kāf.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Innā is shortened from innana by deleting one nūn.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Iyyākum is coordinated with the subject of inna; coordination by syntactic position would instead use antum and would make guidance apply only to the first group.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو العباس | prefers | Abū al-ʿAbbās allows the guidance phrase to apply to the first group; the wording rhetorically presses an opponent to see that one side must be right and the other mistaken.
[NAHHAS:v3p345/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو العباس | holds | The construction resembles saying I will do one thing and you another, and one of us is mistaken, while leaving the listener to recognize which one.
[RUMMANI:v1p104#2/r1] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | Hyperbole enlarges a meaning by departing from the language's ordinary form; one class uses intensified adjective patterns, such as رحمان from راحم, to express God's all-encompassing mercy.
[RUMMANI:v1p104#2/r2] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | Other intensified patterns include فعال, فعول, فعيل, مفعل, and مفعال, illustrated by غفار, غفور, قدير, مدعس, and منحار; رحمان is reserved for God because its meaning encompasses all things.
[RUMMANI:v1p104#2/r6] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | A disputant may frame speech as uncertainty to be fair and strengthen the argument: either side may be guided or astray; the conditional claim about a son follows this pattern.
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The author distinguishes pairing, which answers a word or act with a related counterpart, from verbal appropriateness, where related wording recurs in a new sense. | mentions 2:194, 3:54, 9:67, 22:19
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Taṣrīf varies a word across related senses and varies a meaning through different expressions; the author illustrates the former with forms of الملك and the latter with repeated tellings of Moses' story.
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Taḍmīn conveys a meaning without naming it explicitly, either through a word's structure or because the phrase's meaning entails it; this is a form of concision.
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The basmala implicitly teaches beginning actions in God's name, honoring or seeking blessing through it.
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Mubālagha expresses abundance through emphatic word forms such as raḥmān, ghaffār, shakūr, ghafūr, raḥīm, and qadīr, or through broad and extreme expressions.
[BAQILLANI:v1p271/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Quran's formulation, “we or you are on guidance or manifest error,” is listed among examples of rhetorical hyperbole.
[HAMASA:v1p202/r1] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-Marzūqī reads a Banū Asad poet's denial of perfect generosity as modest self-praise and cites 34:24 as a tactful way to present one's own and another's positions.
[THALABI:v8p87#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The question-and-answer argument concedes that God provides sustenance from heaven and earth.
[THALABI:v8p87#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | “Either we or you are guided or plainly astray” is a fair-minded form of argument, like saying one of us is lying while knowing which one.
[THALABI:v8p87#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The parties cannot both be on one path: Muhammad and his followers are guided, while those opposing him are astray; the

[THALABI:v8p88/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another view takes أو as meaning and: the believers are guided and their opponents are plainly astray.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi directs readers to the explanation in Yunus and notes that the Meccans already acknowledged God as provider there; this proves that the provider alone deserves worship, unlike idols that provide nothing. | mentions 10:31
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Since the Meccans could not name any provider besides God, the Prophet is commanded to answer that God is the provider, completing the proof against them.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The discourse may split after قل الله: the Meccans ask who provides, the answer ends with God, and then an implicit ثم قل introduces the challenge about guidance and error.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس عن عطاء | reports | Ata reports Ibn Abbas saying the alif in أو is an added connective in the expression.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda paraphrases the paired meaning as: we are surely guided and you are in clear error.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil says one group is guided—the Prophet and his Companions—while the other, the Meccan disbelievers, is in clear error.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p361#2/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra rejects making أو equivalent to واو in Arabic: take one dirham or two permits either one or two, not three as a conjunction reading would imply.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p363/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The intended possibilities are that either we are misguided or rightly guided; God knows His Messenger is guided and the others are astray.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p363/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكسائي والأخفش والمبرد | reports | Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and al-Mubarrad say أو expresses no real doubt here: speakers may state that one of two people is wrong while knowing which one, phrasing a rebuke tactfully.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p363/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الأسود | reports | Abu al-Aswad's poem about loving Ali says he is not wrong if that love is error; al-Wahidi notes the poet was certain it was not error, using this as a rhetorical argument.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p363/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The phrase directs speech toward the more decorous expression when the truth is known, using a deliberately indirect accusation rather than bluntly calling the other party a liar.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p363/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The surface wording shows an alternative, not actual doubt; exegetes prioritized the intended meaning and therefore treated أو as coordinating like واو.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:34:24-26/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The provision from the heavens is rain, and that from the earth is vegetation.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p590#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | After compelling their admission, the Prophet frames the dispute fairly: one party among monotheists and idolaters must be guided and the other plainly astray.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p590#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | This even-handed formulation sounds fair to friend and opponent; the preceding questioning makes clear who is guided, while indirectness advances debate with less quarrel and gradually blunts resistance.
